author: beaver state news
title: Everglades hiker fined after capturing invasive python; citation later dismissed
text:
A Florida hiker who captured an invasive python in Everglades National Park received a $180 fine on June 17, but the citation was later dismissed before reaching a judge.
Yatir Nitzany encountered the python while hiking in Shark Valley at Everglades National Park. He said, “I saw one crawling across the trail. There were children around,” according to Local 10 News. Concerned for safety and noting that the snake had recently eaten, Nitzany decided to capture it and wait for park authorities. “It had a bulge in its belly. The upper part of its body indicating it just killed something and I couldn’t have it on my conscience just to leave it there and just let it go,” he said.
After waiting about 30 minutes, Nitzany said a ranger arrived, took possession of the python, and issued him a $180 citation for handling wildlife without authorization—a requirement under federal park rules even when dealing with invasive species.
Pythons are not native to South Florida and are considered highly destructive to native animal populations. Their presence can create cascading effects throughout local ecosystems already facing pressures from development, pollution, and climate-related threats.
Ron Magill, ambassador/conservation liaison at Zoo Miami, commented on the situation: “At the end of the day, for me, it’s common sense. Unfortunately, it’s not too common anymore.” Magill also called for clearer regulations so individuals are not penalized during unusual encounters with invasive species: “My goal now is to do whatever I can to change this law,” he said, “to make sure there is a caveat in this law so that people like Nitzany are not punished for doing the right thing in the environment.” Nitzany reflected on his experience by saying, “I regret asking for help.”
